title: Money Never Sleeps: Maximizing Liquidity Mining Yields in Decentralized Finance

problem.claim: Selecting a liquidity mining solution with maximal yields requires coordinating exchange and deposit transactions while satisfying exchange, minimum, deposit, and budget constraints.

gap.claim: Selecting the most profitable liquidity mining solution is challenging because there are many candidate solutions.

contributions.claim: The paper defines the yield maximization liquidity mining problem, which seeks a maximal-yield solution under minimum, exchange, deposit, and budget constraints.
The paper establishes that the YMLM problem is NP-hard and has no algorithm with a constant approximation ratio.
The paper proposes the YMLM_GD and YMLM_SK algorithms with parameterized approximation ratios.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on real and synthetic datasets report that the proposed approaches outperform baselines in yields.

narrative_sequence.summary: Decentralized finance has increased attention to liquidity mining, where users deposit cryptocurrency pairs into pools to earn yields.
Constructing a liquidity mining solution requires exchange and deposit transactions subject to multiple constraints, and choosing the most profitable solution is difficult.
The paper defines YMLM as maximizing yields over feasible liquidity mining solutions.
The paper gives hardness and approximation-limit results and proposes two algorithms with parameterized approximation ratios.
Experiments on real and synthetic datasets report higher yields than baselines.

source_observation.claim: The solution space combines exchange and deposit decisions under exchange, minimum, deposit, and budget constraints.

interpretation.claim: Liquidity allocation can be modeled as constrained yield optimization rather than as isolated pool selection.

application.claim: For similar allocation problems, formulate transaction or resource choices and feasibility constraints jointly before optimizing the objective.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify when the proposed algorithms' parameterized approximation ratios are preferable or how they behave outside the reported datasets.

unknowns: The abstract does not provide the algorithms' approximation-ratio formulas or parameter definitions.
The abstract does not report dataset sizes, baseline identities, experimental settings, or quantitative yield improvements.
